headline: Zelensky in Berlin after a deadly strike, supermarket fridge hacks hit Germany, and the EU clears JD.com's MediaMarktSaturn deal

stories.title: Zelensky makes a surprise visit to Berlin after a deadly strike on an aid point and a massive overnight attack on Ukraine's grid
facts: Merz announced the visit only this morning at a Berlin IHK breakfast, saying Zelensky would be with him "over lunch"; it had been kept secret for security reasons.

Zelensky says he'll meet the Chancellor, the Federal President and the Bundestag president, and speak at the Berlin Security Conference; his priorities are diplomatic coordination, air defence and the energy sector.
Kyiv wants more Patriot interceptors and help keeping the grid running through winter, a week before the US-led three-way talks in Abu Dhabi.
Overnight Russia hit power plants and substations in Odesa, Cherkasy, Zhytomyr, Vinnytsia, Kharkiv, Dnipro, Chernivtsi, Chernihiv and other regions, according to Zelensky.
The death toll from Russia's strike on an aid distribution at a school in Komyshuvakha (Zaporizhzhia region) has risen to at least 26 per Zelensky, up from 18 last night; 27 people are still missing.
About 3,400 extra police are on duty in Berlin, with parts of the government district and City West closed and disruptions on the U5 and the Ringbahn.
stories.whyItMatters: Germany is Ukraine's biggest European backer, and this visit sets up air-defence and energy help right before the next round of peace talks.

stories.title: The supermarket fridge hacks have reached Germany: four stores in NRW and Bavaria
facts: Two CAP markets (Wuppertal and Wetter-Volmarstein), a Rewe in Raesfeld and an Edeka in Reisbach had their cooling switched to heating overnight, and large amounts of food were thrown away.
In Reisbach the units were heated to 50 °C overnight into Monday, according to heise.
Police in Niederbayern are investigating but haven't confirmed a cyberattack yet, and it's unclear who is behind it.
It follows the wave of manipulated fridges and freezers in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden and Ireland from yesterday; Zeit reports the EU Commission is concerned.
stories.whyItMatters: What looked like a Benelux and Nordic problem is now hitting German chains, so connected refrigeration controls are clearly a live target.

stories.title: EU clears JD.com's takeover of MediaMarktSaturn owner Ceconomy, with 10 years of conditions
facts: The Commission approved the deal under the Foreign Subsidies Regulation after finding JD.com got preferential financing, tax breaks and grants from China.
JD.com must deal with Ceconomy on market terms, including any financing, to prevent cross-subsidies.
It must also offer its warehousing, logistics and tech services to rival retailers on the same terms it gives Ceconomy.
The commitments run for 10 years and an independent trustee will monitor them; China had threatened countermeasures over the probe in August.
Ceconomy says this was the last outstanding approval and the deal will close in the coming days; the offer values Ceconomy at about €2.2bn.
stories.whyItMatters: Europe's biggest electronics retailer is about to be Chinese-owned, and this is a showcase use of the EU's new foreign-subsidy rules.

stories.title: First reserve power plant auction goes entirely to gas, mostly RWE and LEAG
facts: The Bundesnetzagentur awarded 11 contracts totalling about 5,160 MW in its first auction for backup capacity against short-term power shortages.
Ten went to RWE and LEAG (including its subsidiary Gaskraftwerk Leipheim), and one to Stadtwerke Karlsruhe.
Every award went to gas plants, which are meant to secure supply from November 2031.
Spiegel notes LEAG plans to convert old lignite plants to gas, with electricity customers paying for it.
stories.whyItMatters: This sets who builds Germany's backup power for the 2030s, and power customers will end up footing the bill.

stories.title: Schaeffler cuts 3,460 jobs and closes German sites
facts: The auto and industrial supplier is cutting 3,460 jobs worldwide, 2,660 of them in Germany.
Four German sites will close; heise counts 16 sites affected and five closures overall.
Schaeffler expects to save €300m a year from 2030, with one-off costs of about €480m.
stories.whyItMatters: It's another big cut in Germany's struggling auto supply chain.

facts.text: Apple confirms its mercenary-spyware warnings, which also reached German politicians, went out on October 29 to users in 99 countries.
Bomb threats hit flights from UK airports; two planes were checked in Warsaw (Modlin) and one in Murcia.
MI5 won't face contempt charges despite admitting it gave false evidence to three courts in the Agent X case; police may still look at officers for misconduct.
Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel, 30, has died after a collision with FC Andorra's goalkeeper.
NASA's 3,200-pound Swift observatory, launched in 2004, re-enters this week; much of it won't survive and the risk is low.
The White House refuses to release documents on how it vets threats from new AI models, citing national security in a lawsuit.
Correctiv reports a second data leak at NIUS, exposing data of about 42,000 newsletter subscribers.
Researchers found hemoglobin-related biomolecules in a dinosaur leg bone for the first time.
The CDU will decide next week on its candidate for Bundespräsidentin, and Merz says a draft law banning expropriation of housing companies is ready.

facts.text: Siemens Simatic IoT2050 devices are being pulled into a botnet via CVE-2026-58115 (CVSS 10), which was patched in August.
Affinity is coming to Linux; Canva says it's in active development but gives no date.
Apple Intelligence launches in China with iOS 27.3; the developer beta comes Wednesday and the release in December.
The 16GB Raspberry Pi 5 now costs $385 after another $80 hike, up from $120 at launch in January 2025.
PostHog writes up why it's moving off DuckDB.
Mozilla's Firefox security and privacy newsletter for Q3 is out.
Google is rolling out a fix for Pixel Watch battery drain.
